entries.text: Google DeepMind's Gemini 4 Carbon tops AI benchmark with strong security focus
our strongest model with state-of-the-art cybersecurity and long horizon capabilities

DeepMind unveiled Gemini 4 Carbon, the top‑scoring model on the v5.0 AI Index and a leader on security benchmarks, while Google also rolled out Gmail‑sourced autofill in Chrome and OpenAI expanded into ServiceNow and Oracle workflows
Google’s Gemini 4 Carbon tops AI security benchmarks and launches with limited access for cyber‑defense partners.
Chrome’s new AI‑driven autofill pulls relevant details from Gmail to auto‑populate web forms, with encryption and user controls.
OpenAI’s models are now integrated into ServiceNow and Oracle products, letting employees handle tickets, develop code and assess security within ChatGPT.
Anthropic’s new reporting suite gives enterprises detailed cost and workflow insights to manage rapidly rising AI spend.
Cursor's Agent SDK lets teams code, test, and deploy custom development agents in a single step, streamlining workflow automation.
Google DeepMind announced Gemini 4 Carbon on 28 October 2026 as its newest frontier model.
The model is positioned as the company’s strongest offering, emphasizing advanced cybersecurity and long‑horizon reasoning capabilities.
It follows the Gemini 4 Argon release two weeks earlier and will initially be provided to a limited set of cyber‑defense partners through the Fairwind Program.
Gemini 4 Carbon achieved the top rank on the v5.0 Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index with a score of 59, surpassing competitors such as Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT‑6 Astra.
On the SEC‑bench Pro vulnerability‑finding benchmark it scored 88.2%, while it reached 54.8% on ExploitGym and 71.0% on CWE‑bench for patching tasks.
Internally the model reduced misalignment and fabrication rates in live coding tests and can run for days on complex, multi‑step engineering problems.
Pricing mirrors Argon at $2 per million input tokens, $10 per million output tokens, with cached input tokens discounted by 95%.
The model builds on Gemini 4 Argon’s architecture but adds stronger safeguards and longer context handling to support sustained agentic workflows.
Google is engaging with the U.S. government’s voluntary pre‑release testing to refine guardrails before broader release to developers and consumers.
This incremental rollout reflects a cautious approach to deploying powerful AI in security‑sensitive environments.
Google DeepMind unveils Gemini 4 Carbon
Google announced that Chrome will now use its Gemini‑powered Personal Intelligence to pull information from users' Gmail when filling online forms.
The feature launches on Wednesday for desktop users in the United States and for iOS and Android Chrome apps that include Gemini.

entries.text: Users can enable or disable the enhanced autofill in Chrome settings.

The updated autofill can suggest data such as flight confirmation numbers, membership IDs, tracking numbers, order numbers, addresses, phone numbers, and credit‑card details by scanning relevant emails.
It builds on earlier enhancements that already drew names, passport numbers, email addresses, and physical addresses from Google Accounts and Google Wallet.
All suggested data remains encrypted and users retain control over what the feature can access.
Autofill has long helped users avoid typing repetitive information, but it traditionally relied on data stored locally or in basic account profiles.
By linking to Gmail, Chrome leverages the large amount of transactional information most people receive by email, similar to how Apple auto‑fills verification codes from SMS messages.

entries.text: This move deepens Chrome's integration into Google's broader AI ecosystem, encouraging users to stay within the platform.
Chrome adds Gmail‑sourced autofill
OpenAI announced expanded integrations with ServiceNow and Oracle on 27 and 28 October 2026 respectively, bringing its models into enterprise workflow tools.
The partnerships add ChatGPT, Codex and other OpenAI models to ServiceNow products and to Oracle applications accessed through ChatGPT.
Both companies say the goal is to let employees use AI for development, security and routine tasks without leaving their core platforms.
ServiceNow will embed OpenAI models and agents across its workflow suite, enabling users to query incidents, assess change risk and update records directly inside ChatGPT.
The integration uses ServiceNow’s Action Fabric to enforce existing business rules and permissions, so actions respect each organization’s configuration.
A preview also lets on‑call engineers view alerts and assign work within the chat interface.

Oracle’s tie‑up brings its applications and data into ChatGPT and powers new Oracle services with OpenAI models, extending ChatGPT Work and Codex to its 130,000 active ChatGPT users and 95,000 Codex users.
Oracle’s recruiting team reports that tasks that once required two to four days now take 15–20 minutes with ChatGPT Work.
Enterprise software often requires users to switch between multiple tools, which can slow down incident response and development cycles.
By embedding AI directly into workflow platforms, companies aim to reduce context switching and automate routine steps, making processes faster and more consistent.
OpenAI’s models provide natural‑language understanding and code generation capabilities that can be applied to tasks such as ticket triage, code scaffolding and security risk assessment.
OpenAI models added to ServiceNow and Oracle workflows
Anthropic announced a suite of reporting tools on Wednesday to let enterprise managers see how much token spend costs and where workflows break down.
The features let teams view production, cost and recommendations for improvement.
Anthropic also introduced pooled group budgets to help control token usage.
The new tools draw on internal analytics and employee surveys to break down a team’s work over a chosen date range.
Reports show what was produced, the monetary cost and points where processes failed, and they do not use the data for model training by default.
Anthropic’s move follows strong financial results, including operating profit in Q2 and 900% net revenue retention from Q3 2025 to Q3 2026.
Enterprise customers have been demanding clearer ROI on AI tools as many Fortune 500 firms see limited gains.

entries.text: A recent Jellyfish survey of 276,000 developers found Anthropic’s Claude Code responsible for about a third of proposed code changes and its spending now equals roughly 2% of total engineering cost, up 10‑fold this year.
The reporting suite aims to help CFOs manage this rapid cost growth.
Anthropic adds reporting tools for enterprise AI spend
Cursor announced the Agent SDK on 28 October 2026, a framework for building software‑development agents in code.
The SDK lets teams create agents that react to events such as pull‑request submissions, compliance checks, or incident investigations.
Teams can deploy these agents to Cursor infrastructure with a single command, treating them like any other software project.
The Agent SDK provides templates and integrates with GitHub, GitLab, and Bitbucket, enabling agents to assess change risk, route reviews, and automatically approve compliant updates.
A Cursor team built a knowledge‑base reviewer called kb‑reviewer in about a day; it now runs on every PR, flags contradictions, cites source notes, and prompts engineers to resolve issues.
The platform also supports handing tasks to specialized sub‑agents, parallel execution, built‑in evals, and event replay for reliable workflow testing.
Software teams often rely on generic tools or custom scripts to automate repetitive development tasks, which can be misaligned with their unique processes.

By exposing a programmable SDK, Cursor allows teams to codify their own policies and integrate automation directly into existing version‑control events, reducing friction and increasing consistency across the development lifecycle.
This approach mirrors broader trends toward infrastructure‑as‑code for DevOps pipelines.
